through the control of liquor retail sales and high excise taxes has aided in slowing growth and has been an impediment to expansion. Despite this, solid growth in demand for Canadian products in the United States and a boom in craft spirits consumption has mitigated this drop, as did increased

alcohol consumption amid the pandemic. Revenue is expected to climb at a CAGR of 1.7% to $2.1 billion over the five years to 2025, including a forecast boost of 0.8% in 2025 alone as consumption of alcohol continues its long-term decline. Domestic distilleries endure steep competition from foreign

producers that have high Canadian market penetration. This is because reputable brands are preferred over unknown spirit brands by Canadian consumers. Consumer trends have shifted demand toward domestic craft spirits, fuelled by changing tastes parallel to those with craft beer, in addition to

growing disposable income that enables consumers to spend on premium craft spirits. This trend has been the main source of growth and has led to a massive influx of small craft distilleries. Similar trends in the United States have boosted exports of spirits to the neighbouring country and have

aided revenue since the export market is the most important for enterprises in an industry where domestic sales are heavily regulated. Reputable Canadian brands, including Canadian Club and JP Wiser's, have expanded their market share in the United States. Along with thriving revenue, industry

profit has grown despite higher input costs as premiumization has increased sales of more profitable spirits, while distilleries have also successfully passed on higher input costs. Distilleries are also expected to continue growing in the coming years as the economy continues its post-pandemic

expansion. The number of enterprises will keep growing as the industry expands and exports will continue to strengthen amid the continued growth of demand in the United States. The most significant threat to the industry will originate from the potential for higher excise taxes and government

regulation, in addition to the threat of reduced consumption. Overall, revenue is expected to expand at a CAGR of 0.9% over the next five years to reach $2.2 billion in 2030. Manufacturing In Canada • NAICS-Canada 312140 Distilleries in Canada 4 www.ibisworld.com July 2025 Performance Key

Craft distilleries have gained popularity and reshaped consumer expectations • Over the past five years, demand for local, small-batch spirits has soared. Distilleries like Sheringham Distillery in British Columbia and Dillon’s Small Batch Distillers in Ontario have built strong brands by

emphasizing handcrafted techniques and regionally sourced botanicals. This growth reflects a broader cultural shift toward authenticity, transparency, and quality in alcohol consumption. • This trend is important because it has allowed small producers to bypass the traditional barriers of scale

and compete with legacy brands by creating direct emotional connections with their audiences. Many of these distillers offer personalized customer experiences that build Manufacturing In Canada • 31214CA Distilleries in Canada 6 www.ibisworld.com July 2025 lasting loyalty, something large

producers struggle to replicate. • The growth of craft distilling has diversified the industry’s offerings, introducing products like lavender gin, maple liqueurs, and smoked whiskies. For example, Ironworks Distillery in Nova Scotia has gained attention for its nautical-themed spirits and unique

finishing techniques using rum barrels on ships. • In response, distilleries have embraced immersive branding strategies, hosted farm-to-bottle tours and leveraged collaborations with local artisans or restaurants. These efforts not only boost visibility but create compelling value propositions

that resonate with today’s values- driven consumers. Consumers are drinking less alcohol but spending more on premium spirits • Canadians have embraced the “less but better” philosophy. As overall alcohol consumption decreases, premium spirits are outperforming lower-end products. Brands like

Forty Creek Whisky and Lot No. 40 have capitalized on this by offering small-batch or single-barrel expressions that command higher price points and deliver richer storytelling. • This trend matters because it enables producers to maintain or grow profitability even as volume declines.

Premiumization aligns with lifestyle shifts toward health, intentional indulgence and sustainable consumption, positioning high-quality spirits as occasional luxuries rather than everyday staples. • It has encouraged producers to innovate in aging, distillation and finishing techniques. Alberta

Distillers, for instance, has developed a premium rye that earned international recognition. This shows how Canadian producers are competing globally by offering bold flavors, complex aging processes, and standout packaging. • Distilleries are now launching limited releases and reserve lines to

reinforce exclusivity and attract discerning consumers. Some, like Compass Distillers in Halifax, even age their spirits in barrels from local wineries, creating terroir-driven products that blend regional identities and justify their premium positioning. The pandemic and policy changes

transformed how distilleries reach consumers • COVID-19 forced many Canadian distilleries to rethink their operations. When bars and restaurants closed, producers like Taynton Bay Spirits in British Columbia and Strathcona Spirits in Alberta pivoted quickly to offer online ordering, contactless

curbside pickup, and local delivery—new models that sustained revenue during lockdowns. • The crisis prompted temporary provincial reforms. For example, Ontario allowed distilleries to deliver directly to consumers, which was previously prohibited under strict liquor board rules. This opened the

door to new sales channels that provided better profit and more direct customer engagement, even beyond the pandemic. • The shift to digital commerce proved long-lasting. Brands began offering virtual tastings, subscription boxes and cocktail kits. Spirit of York in Toronto launched a sleek online

store, helping them maintain visibility and sales while suspending in-person experiences—an approach that is still generating revenue today. • Distilleries have since invested in permanent e-commerce infrastructure, digital marketing and packaging logistics. Many are now advocating for continued

policy reform, arguing that permanent direct-to-consumer models are vital for small business survival and help them compete with global companies in a more accessible marketplace. Manufacturing In Canada • 31214CA Distilleries in Canada 7 www.ibisworld.com July 2025 Volatility Moderate What

influences industry volatility? Economic expansion will support revenue growth • Distillers in Canada are reliant on macroeconomic trends. While alcohol is very popular, demand for alcoholic beverages, including spirits, can be elastic and reduced in tough economic times. • If per capita

disposable income and consumer spending are on the rise, then consumers will be more willing to expand their spirits purchases by buying more and higher-end products. • This trend reverses when growth slows and disposable income shrinks. Canadians will tighten their budgets and reduce nonessential

purchases when necessary, including of spirits and alcoholic beverages. Distillers are reliant on consumer tastes • Per capita alcohol consumption is one of the most important trends to follow for Canadian distilleries, as it measures how much alcohol Canadians are consuming. • Consumption peaked

in the early 2010s and has steadily declined in the years since, though it did inch upward in 2020 amid the COVID-19 pandemic. • If Canadians consume less alcohol, revenue is at risk of shrinking as they will make fewer purchases, while the opposite is true when consumption jumps. Changes in

regulation can influence trends • Canada enforces strict regulations on alcohol across the entire supply chain, from production facilities to retail outlets. Any changes in these rules may affect the revenue streams of domestic distilleries. • When lawmakers ease restrictions on the sale and

distribution of spirits, distilleries stand to benefit. Some provinces still prohibit direct retail sales at distillery locations, so deregulation could expand market access and drive revenue growth within the sector. • Increased regulatory flexibility typically leads to more opportunities for

distilleries to connect with consumers. Broader distribution channels can help companies boost sales volumes and potentially increase market share, especially in provinces with more stringent regulations. Manufacturing In Canada • 31214CA Distilleries in Canada 8 www.ibisworld.com July 2025

lowering water consumption, minimizing greenhouse gas emissions and reducing packaging waste. Sustainability will no longer be optional; it will be a key factor in long-term competitiveness and consumer trust. • This matters because climate-conscious consumers are now a major demographic,

especially among millennials and Gen Z. Brands that fail to demonstrate environmental responsibility risk alienating these buyers and falling behind distilleries that actively promote clean production and ethical sourcing practices. • Government policies and environmental regulations are expected

to tighten, with incentives for green innovation and penalties for excessive waste or energy use. Distilleries that prepare early will benefit from financial and reputational advantages, while others may be forced into costly retrofits later. • Many distilleries are already making moves, such as

installing energy-efficient stills, switching to renewable energy, or adopting biodegradable labels. In the years ahead, businesses should consider closed-loop water systems, carbon-offset partnerships and transparent sustainability reporting to differentiate themselves and future-proof their

consumer engagement in the distillery sector is going digital. Canadian distilleries will need to expand their online presence through e-commerce platforms, mobile-friendly websites and robust social media strategies to reach digitally native consumers and compete in a more tech-driven retail

environment. • This trend is important because traditional retail channels, including liquor stores and on-premise venues, are limited in their ability to tell a brand’s story. Digital tools allow distilleries to personalize interactions, create immersive brand experiences and build long-term

relationships with customers beyond the point of sale. • Online marketing and sales will be supported by backend investments in automation, CRM platforms and data analytics. These tools help track consumer preferences, optimize product offerings and identify regional or seasonal trends—allowing

producers to be more agile and targeted in their approach. • Forward-thinking distilleries are already integrating QR code-enabled labels, offering virtual tastings and launching loyalty apps. Over the next five years, businesses that embrace digital innovation—from augmented reality packaging to

AI-driven customer service—will build deeper engagement and unlock new revenue streams. Global demand for Canadian premium spirits is expected to accelerate • Canadian premium spirits—especially rye whisky, gin and specialty liqueurs—are gaining traction in international markets because of their

craftsmanship, heritage and clean reputation. As global consumers seek unique, high-quality offerings, demand for Canadian-made products is expected to increase sharply over the next five years. • This trend is important because international expansion offers distilleries access to faster-growing

markets outside of Canada’s mature domestic environment. Countries across Asia-Pacific and Europe, in particular, are showing rising interest in craft and boutique spirits from credible and transparent origins like Canada. • Exporting helps distilleries diversify revenue streams, reduce reliance

on domestic economic cycles and build brand prestige globally. However, success in international markets requires compliance with foreign regulations, strategic partnerships and effective cross-cultural marketing that highlights Canada's identity and product distinctiveness. • To seize this

opportunity, Canadian distilleries must invest in international distribution channels, work with global influencers or importers and secure certifications or appellation protections where possible. Participation in global expos, trade missions and industry awards can also elevate visibility and

validate product quality to overseas buyers. Life Cycle Growth Why is the industry growing? Contribution to GDP Industry value added for Canadian distilleries is growing more rapidly than the overall Canadian economy. This growth is being driven by strong trends such as premiumization and the

increasing popularity of craft spirits, both of which have significantly boosted revenue and profit for Canadian distillery businesses in recent years. Market Saturation The market for distilleries is becoming more saturated as the craft spirits boom continues to gain momentum. Many new entrants

have joined over the past few years, increasing competition and this trend is expected to persist. Established brands as well as innovative startups are striving to capture a share of this growing market. Innovation Innovation is ticking up among distilleries, particularly among smaller craft

operations. These artisanal producers can more easily experiment with unique flavors, unusual ingredients, and creative processes to set their products apart. Meanwhile, the popularity of ready-to-drink cocktails continues to grow, as consumers seek convenience and variety in their beverage

options. Consolidation There isn’t a sign of consolidation activity, as enterprises are growing more quickly than establishments. This trend suggests that the market is still in a growth phase, with new businesses continuing to emerge. Additionally, it indicates that market saturation has not yet

been reached at this stage. Technology & Systems Distilling alcohol is a highly mechanized process, typically requiring significant capital investment in specialized equipment to increase efficiency and precision. However, some smaller craft distilleries lack the financial resources for such

generating nearly a third of total distillery revenue nationwide. Crafted from mashed grains such as corn and rye, it is the only Canadian spirit with legal protection under appellation laws, which regulate its production standards. • Canadian whisky must adhere to strict regulations, including

being distilled and aged exclusively within Canada for at least three years and maintaining a minimum alcohol content of 40.0%. These requirements ensure a consistent standard and protect the product’s distinct Canadian identity in both domestic and international markets. • Trade in whisky between

Canada and the United States remains robust. Canadian consumers frequently purchase American-made Tennessee whisky and bourbon, while US consumers favor Canadian brands like Crown Royal. This cross-border exchange highlights the deep mutual appreciation for distinctive whisky styles and

strengthens the economic ties between the two countries’ spirits industries. Vodka is a steady source of revenue • Vodka is the second-most popular spirit produced in Canada. It is distilled mainly from cereal grains or potatoes. Both flavoured and unflavoured varieties are available, broadening

its reach within the alcoholic beverage market and helping secure a consistent demand. • Major vodka brands on the Canadian market—such as Absolut, Skyy, Smirnoff, Belvedere and Grey Goose—are imported, which limits the overall market share captured by Canadian distilleries. Domestic vodka brands

have yet to achieve similar recognition on a national scale, affecting the segment’s potential revenue. • Vodka’s neutral flavour profile allows for wide versatility in cocktails and has driven a surge in available flavoured options. Although Canadian vodka production has grown in recent years,

overall revenue from vodka sales remains stable rather than climbing significantly. Canadian rum has declined in popularity • Canadian rum has seen a notable decrease in popularity, primarily because of the country’s lack of domestic sugarcane production. Since sugarcane and its byproducts must be

imported, production costs tend to be higher, making it difficult for local rum producers to compete with larger, well-established brands from regions like the Caribbean and Latin America. • The local rum market is primarily led by the Newfoundland and Labrador Liquor Corporation, a crown

corporation known for manufacturing Newfoundland Screech and other spirits. Despite its strong regional recognition, the corporation faces challenges as imported brands continue to attract significant consumer attention. • Recent market trends indicate a shift toward premiumization, with more

consumers opting for imported, higher-quality rums instead of local varieties. This evolution has contributed to a shrinking revenue share for Canadian-made rum, highlighting the competitive pressures from global brands. Liqueurs have climbed as a share of revenue • Liqueurs—spirits flavored with

fruits, herbs, spices and sweeteners—have increased their share of industry revenue across Canada. Characterized by a syrupy taste and minimal aging, they're appealing to a wider demographic looking for variety in alcoholic beverages. • The market offers an extensive range of liqueur types,

allowing consumers to match nearly any taste preference. This versatility makes liqueurs a frequent choice in both cocktail recipes and as stand-alone aperitifs. • The growing trend of cocktail culture in Canada continues to push up demand for liqueurs. Industry experts note that this momentum is

likely to persist, helping liqueurs maintain a rising segment of the beverage market's overall revenue. Gin has had a renaissance of popularity • Gin sales in Canada have seen significant growth recently, with distilleries' revenue rising by over 50% between fiscal 2019 and Manufacturing In Canada

are choosing higher-end, higher- margin gin over lower-cost options, increasing profitability for producers and shifting market dynamics in favor of premium categories. • Small distilleries have played a key role by offering unique flavors and niche products that appeal particularly to younger

demographics. This innovation has not only expanded the consumer base but is also expected to sustain strong sales moving forward. All other spirits are a small share of revenue • Canadian distilleries derive only a small fraction of their revenue from spirits such as grain alcohol, tequila and

cordials. The majority of these products, especially tequila, tend to be imported, which limits their ability to contribute significantly to domestic revenue streams. • The broad variety of products within this category has resulted in minimal revenue growth for Canadian distilleries. Imports

dominate the market for certain spirits, leaving little room for domestic producers to expand their share within this segment. • Market trends point to sustained or even increased reliance on imported spirits, ensuring that revenue from these categories will stay low for Canadian distilleries in

pre-mixed beverages deliver a variety of flavour profiles, responding to growing consumer demand for convenience and diversity in alcoholic drinks. • RTD cocktails allow consumers to enjoy classic favourites like margaritas and cosmopolitans without any preparation, making them a practical option

for at-home gatherings and social events. The appeal lies in their portability and consistent taste, setting them apart from traditional mixed drinks. • The rise of canned cocktails increases competition in the alcoholic beverage sector. Beer and wine producers are entering the RTD space,

intensifying the race for market share and potentially reshaping consumer preferences across several beverage categories. Craft spirits have ushered in new products • The rise of craft spirits mirrors the earlier craft beer boom, as independent distilleries attract more consumers and expand market

diversity. Their emergence offers drinkers an increasing array of choices compared to what was previously available. • Many small-batch distilleries experiment with unique flavour profiles and target consumers interested in regional, artisanal labels. This trend caters to the growing demand for

industry’s markets? Liquor stores dominate revenue shares • A highly regulated framework restricts Canadian distilleries’ ability to sell directly to consumers. While a handful of provinces permit some direct sales, the majority prohibit this practice, reinforcing the dominance of

government-controlled outlets. • Provincial liquor control boards play a central role in the retail distribution of alcohol. These government bodies not only set regulations but also operate most retail locations, resulting in limited alternatives for spirits sales at the consumer level. • Legal

mandates require that spirits sales flow through centralized government entities. In British Columbia, the Liquor Distribution Branch manages this process, while Ontario relies on the Liquor Control Board, emphasizing the boards’ significant sway over the entire spirits market. Wholesalers are a

steady revenue source • Liquor wholesalers consistently generate close to twenty percent of distilleries' total income. While direct retail sales lead the market because of strict government regulations, wholesalers maintain an important and reliable role within the industry’s financial ecosystem.

• In many cases, wholesalers function as intermediaries, connecting independent retailers, restaurants, bars and nightclubs to distillery products. Their position facilitates smoother distribution but is tightly linked to the performance of the hospitality sector. • Although the share of revenue

coming from wholesalers usually holds steady, it can fluctuate as economic conditions impact restaurants and venues. When these sectors perform strongly, demand for wholesale distribution tends to rise, supporting distillery sales. Bars, clubs and consumers comprise the remainder of revenue •

Sales to restaurants, bars, nightclubs and direct consumers contributed less than 10% of total revenue in 2024, highlighting their marginal role compared to other major markets within the sector. • Provincial regulations across most regions impose strict limits on direct-to-consumer liquor sales,

restricting consumer access and reducing potential revenue streams from these channels. • Most hospitality establishments, including bars and restaurants, rely on wholesalers rather than purchasing directly from distilleries, further limiting the revenue potential from these direct commercial

largest importer of spirits into Canada is the United States. The USMCA facilitates free trade between the two countries, in addition to Mexico, which is the third-largest importer. The long land border between the two countries also facilitates frequent trade. • Many large distilleries are based

in the United States and choose to import their goods to Canada, rather than produce them domestically, which adds to the high level of import penetration that Canadian distilleries face. Many different countries import different goods • While the United States imports a large share of distilled

spirits, the UK and Mexico each comprise more than 10.0% of the total, closely followed by Ireland. • Mexico is one of the fastest-growing importers of spirits to Canada. Tequila, which is made from agave, a plant that does much better in hot climates than the more temperate environment in Canada,

is one of the country's biggest spirits. • In the UK, gin and Scotch whiskey are popular exports, including Gordon's, Bombay Sapphire and Tanqueray gins, as well as Dewar's Scotch. Whiskey is also a popular export from Ireland, as Jameson is based in Dublin. Exports High Increasing What are the

industry’s export trends? Exports are almost exclusively to the United States • Most exported distilled spirits from Canada are bound for the United States. Similar to imports, the long land border between the two countries, in addition to the USMCA, facilitates free trade. • Its size also creates

a significantly larger consumer market, even if trends in the individual consumer market are similar. This influences Canadian distilleries to export their products to the United States. • Canadian whiskies, including Seagram's and Crown Royal, are very popular in the country. Whisky represents

nearly one-third of all alcohol produced in Canada and differs from many products, namely bourbon, produced in the United States. Most other exports are to the Pacific Rim • Most of the remaining exports are taken by countries in Asia, in addition to Australia. British Columbia has a high level of

access to these countries, which include Japan, Vietnam and Australia. • Canadian distilleries benefit from trade agreements and favourable tariffs with Pacific Rim countries, fostering a competitive edge. This has led to a boost in demand for premium Canadian spirits such as whisky and gin.
